abstract.title: SUMMARY
abstract.p: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic is characterized by the emergence of novel variants of concern (VOC) that replace ancestral strains. Here, we dissect the complex selective pressures by evaluating variant fitness and adaptation in human respiratory tissues. We evaluate viral properties and host responses to reconstruct forces behind D614G through Omicron (BA.1) emergence. We observe differential replication in airway epithelia, differences in cellular tropism, and virus-induced cytotoxicity. D614G accumulates the most mutations after infection, supporting zoonosis and adaptation to the human airway. We perform head-to-head competitions and observe the highest fitness for Gamma and Delta. Under these conditions, RNA recombination favors variants encoding the B.1.617.1 lineage 3’ end. Based on viral growth kinetics, Alpha, Gamma, and Delta exhibit increased fitness compared to D614G. In contrast, the global success of Omicron likely derives from increased transmission and antigenic variation. Our data provide molecular evidence to support epidemiological observations of VOC emergence.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: In December of 2019, a novel coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, emerged and rapidly spread across the world, causing the ongoing global COVID-19 pandemic.1 SARS-CoV-2 is a betacoronavirus of the Sarbecovirus subgenus and is closely related to SARS-CoV, a pandemic coronavirus that emerged in 2002–03. As of early 2023, SARS-CoV-2 is estimated to have infected ~700 million individuals and caused nearly 7 million reported deaths and extensive economic losses worldwide. Since the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, the scientific community rapidly developed a variety of novel vaccines and therapeutics, which have greatly alleviated disease severity.2–5

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has been characterized by the continued emergence of new variants encoding adaptive mutations that enhance fitness and transmissibility in humans, leading to “replacement” of the immediate ancestral strain. Early in 2020, a variant encoding a mutation in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein (D614G) swept the globe and replaced the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 strain, 6,7 becoming the progenitor strain of all later variants. The Alpha variant (B.1.1.7) arose in December of 2020,8 along with the Beta variant (B.1.351).9 The Gamma variant (P.1) emerged soon thereafter in January of 2021.10 In April of 2021, the Kappa variant (B.1.617.1) emerged but was quickly replaced by its sister strain, the Delta variant (B.1.617.2).11 The emergence of the Omicron strain (B.1.1.529), which was first identified in November of 2021, heralded a major antigenic shift in the Spike glycoprotein and was ancestral to numerous sub-lineages of Omicron through today.12 Unlike previous variant emergences and replacements, multiple sublineages of Omicron have circulated since its emergence, with a “soup” of variants being observed. The Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron variants were named Variants of Concern (VOC) by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).13,14

Viral fitness is regulated by a variety of virus-host interactions that influence replication, transmissibility, and antigenicity.15 Although information can be gained from population-level data, fitness is a complex trait, and it can be difficult to disentangle the different drivers. During the pandemic, Alpha, Delta, and Omicron were progressively more successful variants, causing successive global strain replacements. This could reflect increases in replication and/or transmissibility; notably, Delta and Omicron emerged after the development of COVID-19 vaccines, and re-infection is possible with these variants, suggesting that antigenic drift may have promoted virus escape from pre-existing immunity. In this context, the Omicron variants contain a particularly large proportion of mutations in the Spike protein, the major driver of antigenicity, compared to other variants.16

In the current study, we studied viral replicative fitness in primary human airway cells derived from the proximal and distal airways, including the alveoli, the primary targets for virus replication in human populations. For each variant, we evaluated viral growth, cellular tropism, the cellular responses upon infection, and viral evolution and adaptation in culture. We also investigated the evolutionary transition states of strain replacement by growing variants in head-to-head competition. We demonstrated subtle differences in virus tropism following infection of primary airway epithelial cells, discrete growth differences, and altered host transcriptomic patterns using single cell sequencing after infection. Moreover, virus evolution rates were reduced in globally successful VOCs, suggesting that adaptive changes enhanced virus infection of primary human airway epithelial cells during the pandemic.

sec.title: SARS-CoV-2 Variant Growth Kinetics in Primary Human Airway Cells
sec.p: Using a panel of clinical isolates, we characterized the growth kinetics of D614G, Alpha (B.1.1.7), Beta (B.1.35.1), Gamma (P.1), Kappa (B.1.617.1), Delta (B.1.617.2), and Omicron (BA.1) strains in primary human airway epithelia cells cultured at an air-liquid interface (ALI) and derived from distinct anatomical compartments from the proximal to distal lung from at least three different patients. In the most proximal region, nasal epithelia (HNE), D614G reached a peak titer of 107 PFU/mL at 96 hpi, a 1.5–2-log higher peak titer as compared with all other variants which peaked earlier. Omicron, which replicated most efficiently during the first 48 hpi, exhibited ~1-log higher titers than other variants at 24hpi. (Figure 1A). In large airway bronchial epithelia (LAE), representing trachea and bronchi, Alpha and Delta also achieved peak titers of 106 PFU/mL at earlier timepoints (72hpi) than D614G (96hpi). The Gamma, Kappa, and Omicron variants clustered together, growing efficiently in the first 24–48 hours post infection (hpi), although with a 1–1.5 log reduction in peak titer at 72 hpi. The Beta variant was least fit in culture, with a 48-hour delay in replication (Figure 1B). In small airway epithelia cells (SAE), representing cells lining the bronchioles, D614G growth was most efficient, achieving 107 PFU/mL at 72 hrs, closely followed by Alpha and Delta. Gamma, Kappa, and Omicron variant growth in SAE remained tightly clustered ~2-logs lower than D614G, and the Beta variant again displayed a substantial growth defect compared to other viruses (Figure 1C). We also infected AT2 alveolosphere organoids, a model of the distal gas exchange region of the human lung,17 with each variant. D614G, Gamma, and Kappa variants replicated most efficiently in this model (Figure 1D), with Omicron and Beta displayed substantially attenuated growth kinetics compared to all other variants. As a control, we also infected commonly used A549-hACE2 cells with each variant. Wide variation in viral growth was observed as has been previously reported; some similarities were observed in comparison to primary culture infections, including generally efficient replication of D614G and poor replication of Beta (Figure 1E).

Because primary cell cultures are derived from genetically distinct human donors, patient codes encode natural genetic variation reflective of outbred populations. In HNE cells, we observed moderate levels of variation in virus variant growth between different donor codes (Supplemental Figure 1A). Viral growth in LAEs displayed more variable phenotypes, associated with different cell donors and virus strains. D614G growth was the most variable between codes, while Delta displayed the least variation in virus growth (Supplemental Figure 1B). Virus variant growth efficiency in SAE cultures demonstrated important differences, with D614G and Delta achieving 106-107 peak titers with little variability across codes. In contrast, Omicron also showed little variation, but only achieved titers 1–2 logs lower (Supplemental Figure 1C). Although the numbers are small, the homogeneity of Delta and Omicron growth on different codes may reflect a greater ability to infect and replicate in a range of different genetic backgrounds across the proximal and distal lung compartments, although with contrasting efficiencies.

sec.title: SARS-CoV-2 Variants Primarily Infect Ciliated Cells
sec.p: At 96 hours post infection, cells were harvested, and cellular tropism was assessed by whole mount staining and RNAScope (Figure 1F-H). By RNAScope, all variants primarily infected FOXJ1+ ciliated cells and FOXJ1−/SCGB1A1− cells, indicating a preference for ciliated cell infection (Figure 1F, Supplemental Figure 2A). By immunofluorescent staining, the viruses infected approximately 1–15% of cells in culture, primarily α-tubulin+ ciliated cells and α-tubulin+/CCSP+ transitional cells (Figure 1G-H). Although there was variability due to donor variation, there was a trend toward a higher percentage of infected cells in SAE compared to LAE cells. In some infected areas, virus was found in α-tubulin+ cells lacking cilia (Supplemental Figure 2B), possibly indicating ciliocytophthoria, a degenerative ciliated cell process that occurs after infection.18 In Omicron infected SAE cultures, a unique population of α-tubulin−/CCSP− cells were infected, possibly reflecting a novel tropism or loss of marker expression due to infection. The tropism of Beta was similar to the other variants in SAE cells. However, in LAE cells, viral antigen was only observed in one code, in CCSP+ squamous cells (Figure 1H). For most variants, we observed areas with gaps in the tight junction, which may reflect cell death and extrusion. (Supplemental Figure 2C)

sec.title: Omicron Infected Primary Airway Cells Display Distinct Morphologies Compared to Other Variants
sec.p: To directly visualize cell morphology following viral infection, we performed electron microscopy on infected large airway cultures at 72 hours post infection. By scanning electron microscopy (SEM), we observed the formation of large “megacells” coated with virus in D614G infected cultures as previously described; 19 these cells often displayed characteristics of membrane fusion and syncytia formation (Figure 1I, white arrow). Infection with other early variants of concern including Alpha, Beta, and Gamma yielded similar cellular phenotypes (Supplemental Figure 2D). In contrast, Delta and Omicron infected cultures had fewer megacells. Omicron infected cells exhibited increased mucus secretion and abnormal morphologies including extended membrane protrusions (yellow arrows) from infected cells (Figure 1I). We additionally utilized transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to visualize intracellular viral packaging. For most variants, vesicles containing many virion particles were observed (Figure 1I, Supplemental Figure 2D). However, in Omicron infected cells, many vesicles were observed, the majority of which were empty or contained only few virions (Figure 1I, red arrow). This may reflect differences in viral egress, or the plateau of viral growth observed in Omicron-infected cultures after 48 hours.

sec.title: SARS-CoV-2 Variants Cause Substantial Cytotoxicity in Primary Nasal Cells
sec.p: Given the differential responses to infection, we measured whether differences in cytotoxicity were observed following infection with the different SARS-CoV-2 variants. Apical washes collected during the growth curves were analyzed for release of lactase dehydrogenase (LDH), a general marker of cell death.20 In LAE cells, LDH release was observed over the course of 96 hpi after infection with Alpha, Delta, and Omicron variants; Omicron infection was associated with the greatest amount of cell death. No significant LDH release was observed over the course of infection with any variant in SAE cells derived from the bronchioles (Figure 2A). Interestingly, the highest levels of cytotoxicity were observed in HNE cells, with up to 80% cytotoxicity by 96 hpi.21,22 D614G infection led to the greatest cytotoxicity, closely followed by Delta and Omicron infection (Figure 2A). Reports have indicated that the gas exchange regions of the lung have greater innate immune responses than proximal airways, which may explain the observed lack of cytotoxicity in SAE cells.23 The striking differences in LDH signal among airway epithelial cells suggests novel tissue-specific control of SARS-CoV-2 cell based killing mechanisms in the airway.

sec.title: scRNA-seq Reveals Distinct Tropism and Increased Immune Response in Omicron Infected Airway Cells
sec.p: We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) on primary airway cultures infected with D614G, Delta, or Omicron. In combined data from all conditions, airway cells clustered into 15 groups comprising three major cell types: ciliated, secretory, and basal (Figure 2B). Viral infection, as determined by expression of the nucleocapsid gene, was observed in all three major cell types, although relatively little viral gene expression was observed in basal cells (Figure 2C). Strongest viral infection was observed in cluster 9, infected ciliated cells, which displayed a global takeover of cellular transcription by the virus (Supplemental Figure 2D). Gene expression in different clusters revealed that infected secretory (cluster 0), but not infected ciliated cells (cluster 9), displayed robust induction of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) (Figure 2D). We observed some IFITM2 expression in uninfected, but not infected, ciliated cells, although at a lower level than in secretory cells; ISG15, MX2, and IFI27 were strongly upregulated in secretory cells. Infected ciliated cells also had decreased expression of cilia marker genes (Figure 2E). Comparing the variants separately, Delta and D614G infected ciliated cells most efficiently at 48 hours post infection, while Omicron displayed a broader tropism with infection of secretory and basal cell populations in addition to ciliated cell populations. Omicron also led to the highest expression of ISGs ISG15, MX2, and IFI27 in secretory cells (Figure 2F). In contrast to D614G, Omicron viral gene expression generally reduced between 48 and 96 hours post infection (Supplemental Figure 2F). The differential cell tropism, and cell-type specific ISG induction, correlate with the plateau of Omicron viral growth after 48 hours in primary airway cells, while D614G and Delta continue to replicate (Figure 1B-C).

sec.title: Later Variants Display Reduced Mutational Load After Growth in Primary Airway Cells
sec.p: Viral populations derived from clinical samples exist as a quasispecies, encoding mutational swarms. To understand how viral populations are selected or evolve in primary human cells, we sequenced progeny virus from the final 96 hpi timepoint LAE and SAE growth curves. The frequencies of the identified mutations were summed to determine relative mutation load (RML; ∑i=1i=nfi). Progeny D614G virions had the greatest RML; Alpha, Gamma, and Kappa had moderate mutation loads, while Delta, and Omicron had the lowest RML (Figure 3A). When mapped across the viral genome, mutations in D614G, on average, consisted of many low (<10%) frequency mutations spread across the viral genome. Some of the identified mutations have since been observed in human isolates, including ORF3a D27Y, ORF3a T89I, and ORF10 S23F; however, few mutations in Spike were detected. In contrast, the other variants tended to display a few conserved, higher frequency mutations, often non-coding (Figure 3B). Additionally, we observed changes in the frequency of pre-existing mutations in the variants relative to the initial population. The most commonly selected mutation in later variants was nsp6ΔSGF, increasing in frequency in Alpha and Beta viruses after growth in primary airway cells. Progeny sequenced from infected LAE cultures at 14 days post infection displayed the same trends (Supplemental Figure 3). As zoonotic strains oftentimes undergo mutational bursts following host shifts, the rapid evolution of the early D614G strain is consistent with ongoing adaptation to human airway epithelia, while the more contemporary variants had pre-existing adaptation to human airway.

sec.title: Competition Assays Reveal Differences in Replicative Fitness Between SARS-CoV-2 Variants
sec.p: To mimic the transition states between changes in viral dominance, we compared viral replicative fitness head-to-head using competition assays in LAE and SAE cultures. Competitions were performed separately in each cell type and the presented data are a combination of both experiments. Cultures were infected with a 1:1 MOI ratio of viruses, and progeny collected at 5 days to model an infection course (Figure 4A). Of note, although all competitions were performed with a 1:1 mixture by MOI as determined by plaque assay, measured RNA levels at Day 0, especially in Omicron competitions, contained unequal amounts of RNA, indicating a higher viral genome/PFU ratio for Omicron. By comparing the composition of the viral mixture at Day 0 and Day 5 between different competitions, we determined a relative rank order of viral fitness. Gamma was most fit in culture, outcompeting D614G, Alpha, Beta, Kappa, and Delta. Delta and Alpha also outcompeted several other variants including D614G, while D614G and Kappa variants had roughly equivalent fitness phenotypes. Omicron and Beta were outcompeted by D614G. (Figure 4B; Gamma > Delta > Alpha > D614G ~ Kappa > Omicron ~ Beta). Additionally, we performed a subset of competition experiments with a modified setup, passaging every 3 days, to model transmission at peak titer (Supplemental Figure 4A). Results of these competitions were generally similar to the single passage experiment, with high observed fitness for Delta. However, while Omicron was outcompeted by D614G and Alpha in a single passage, no differences in viral fitness were observed in the multi-passage competitions, which is concordant with the relatively efficient replication of Omicron at early timepoints of infection.

To understand whether major fitness differences derive from Spike mutations or elsewhere in the genome, we utilized D614G recombinants encoding the Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron Spike proteins.24–26 In these viruses, the ORF7 gene was removed and replaced with a nLuc reporter gene. Competitions were then performed with each variant Spike against D614G-nLuc with the single passage experimental design (Supplemental Figure 4B). In competition, D614G recombinants encoding the Alpha and Beta Spikes outcompeted the D614G Spike. Although full-length Alpha also outcompeted D614G, full-length Beta did not. Gamma-nLuc and Delta-nLuc had no significant difference in fitness compared to D614G-nLuc, in contrast to the outcome seen with full-length viruses. Lastly, Omicron-nLuc was outcompeted by D614G-nLuc, as was also observed with full-length virus (Figure 4B, Supplemental Figure 4B). Together these data suggest that viral fitness is, in part, affected by Spike mutations. However, given the discordance between full-length and Spike for some variants, mutations elsewhere in the genome also have significant impacts on virus competitive fitness that can exceed contributions from Spike.

sec.title: Evidence of 3’ End Recombination in Mixed Variant Infections
sec.p: Using progeny virions from the last competition time point, genomic RNA was extracted and subjected to high-throughput sequencing, identifying a variety of novel mutations in the virus populations as well as evidence for RNA recombination between strains (Figure 5, Supplemental Figure 5A). Intriguingly, competitions between Kappa and other variants resulted in progeny with altered frequencies of variant marker mutations at the 3’ end of the viral genome, a sign of viral recombination. Specifically, mutations derived from Kappa were over-represented in the 3’ end of the viral genome, while mutations deriving from the other variant were correspondingly under-represented (Figure 5). These findings suggest that the 3’ end of the B.1.617.1 lineage may be positively selected in mixed infections and offer increased competitive fitness. In the Delta vs Omicron competition, there was also a small decrease in the frequency of some Omicron Spike mutations, suggesting a mild fitness disadvantage of these mutations in the absence of pre-existing immunity (Figure 5).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: When the growth of SARS-CoV-2 variants was compared in primary large airway, small airway, and nasal epithelia, several key differences were observed. In lower airway cells, D614G, Alpha, and Delta displayed efficient continued viral replication for 96 hours, whereas Omicron growth peaked at 48 hours. Ciliated cells were the predominant targets of infection, as observed by several independent methodologies. Expression of ciliated markers were reduced after infection, and we also observed dysregulation of cilia and changes to cellular morphology after acute infection as has been previously reported.27–29 The Alpha and Delta variants have been considered more pathogenic,30,31 and this may in part reflect increased or prolonged viral replication. However, we observed the greatest cell death in Omicron infected LAE cultures, suggesting that the reduction in Omicron pathogenesis in humans may be more related to preference for the upper airway or host pre-immune status rather than altered virulence potential, as SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis is associated with replication in the lower airway. Interestingly, the greatest cytotoxicity after infection was observed in nasal epithelial cells, which may partially explain the reported loss of smell in many COVID-19 patients.32 Although there have been reports that Omicron infection causes less anosmia than ancestral strains,33 Omicron infection led to a comparable level of cytotoxicity as other strains in HNE cells in culture.

Although human-to-human transmission cannot be evaluated in primary culture, the ability to replicate in proximal airway cells, especially nasal epithelia, likely influences transmission phenotypes.22 Omicron had substantially improved growth kinetics in the first 48 hours of infection in HNE. Efficient and rapid replication in the nasal epithelium is consistent with the increased transmission dynamics associated with the emergence of the Omicron BA.1 Variant of Concern, especially at early stages of infection before symptomatic onset. Interestingly, it has also been reported that Omicron, in contrast to earlier strains of SARS-CoV-2, is equally as efficient at infecting the pediatric nasal airway as the adult nasal airway, 34 and there is data indicating increased rates of infection in children after the emergence of Omicron.35

While our primary cell culture model does not incorporate adaptive immune responses, these activities play a large role in vivo. Several SARS-CoV-2 variants, including Delta and Omicron, have shifted antigenicity compared to the original zoonosis strain (Supplemental Figure 5B). 36,37 The Delta variant arose in April of 2021, several months after the first introduction of COVID-19 vaccines, although only ~500 million people globally were estimated to have received at least one vaccine dose at that time.38 In contrast, the Omicron variant emerged in November of 2021, at which point ~4 billion people are believed to have been vaccinated, and more were likely to have been previously infected. The greater level of population immunity likely constituted a selective pressure on the virus. The newly emerged Omicron BA.1 strains contained a greater proportion of viral mutations located in the Spike protein,16 the major antigenic target of SARS-CoV-2 adaptive immune responses,39 as compared to previous variants. Omicron has been associated with greater risk of reinfection,40 and in September of 2022, and again in September of 2023, updated bivalent vaccines including Omicron Spike mRNA were introduced to target the novel antigenic signature.41

While the primary cell model system used in this work lacks pre-immune status and immune cell populations, the cultures are immune competent and mount innate immune responses to viral infection, which viruses have evolved ways of avoiding or antagonizing.42 From our scRNA-seq data, we observed two distinct virally infected cell populations – secretory cells that expressed lower concentrations of viral RNAs and higher ISG expression phenotypes, and ciliated cells that had high viral RNA concentrations and little ISG expression. Upregulated ISGs included ISG15, MX2, IFI27, and IFITM2, which have been previously reported to be induced in COVID-19 patients and in cell culture.43–47 Intriguingly, although IFITM2 is canonically known as an antiviral effector, it has also been demonstrated to promote coronavirus infection.45,48 We also observed different tropism preferences for SARS-CoV-2 variants with implications for the host immune response. Notably, Omicron infected secretory cells well, leading to high ISG expression which possibly impeded replication at later time points. In contrast, D614G and Delta preferentially infected ciliated cells, with reduced levels of ISG expression. The preference of early pandemic strains of SARS-CoV-2 for ciliated cells has been previously reported.47 It has been proposed for influenza virus that surviving cells after infection with higher ISG and cytokine stimulation contribute to host lung damage,49 and this cell type may affect the pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2. In contrast, there is evidence that delayed ISG responses leading to greater viral replication correlate with greater pathogenesis in coronavirus infection.50 Studies investigating correlations between interferon responses and disease severity in COVID-19 patients have returned conflicting results,51–53 indicating that the exact effects of Interferon induction and cytokine signaling are complex and require further interrogation.

Evidence points to a zoonotic origin of SARS-CoV-2, as extremely closely related viruses have been found circulating in bat reservoirs in Asia.54–56 After zoonotic transfer to an alternative host, virus evolution rapidly selects for variants that are more efficiently adapted to by-pass replication and transmission bottlenecks within the host.57–59 An example is the initial D614G Spike mutation, which modified the receptor binding domain dynamics, resulting in enhanced infectivity and transmission.6,60 As the virus adapts to a new host over time, it is expected the number of new adaptive mutations will likely plateau. In our experiments, we observed that the parental D614G variant had a relatively high mutation load, with many different mutations observed spread along the length of the genome. Further, there was little overlap between the mutations observed in several independent replicate infections. Many mutations detected in our experiments were not observed in human isolate sequence databases, including the Spike P807R mutation that was observed. However, we did observe some mutations, including ORF3a D27Y, ORF3a T89I, and ORF10 S23F, that have been reported at low frequencies in human viral isolates.61 No data have been reported investigating the functional impacts of these mutations, but an estimate of mutational fitness suggests that ORF3a D27Y is neutral, and ORF3a T89I and ORF10 S23F may slightly increase fitness; Spike P807R is estimated to slightly reduce fitness.62 In contrast, the later variants had reduced mutation loads after growth in primary human cells, supporting the hypothesis that the rate of evolution and adaptation stabilizes over time in the absence of immune pressure. The mutations that were observed in later variants tended to be more conserved between replicates, and some were observed in multiple variants. The most commonly observed change was an increase in the frequency of nsp6ΔSGF in Alpha, Beta, and Gamma variants after growth in primary cells. The nsp6ΔSGF mutation emerged independently in humans in Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Eta, Iota, Lambda, and Omicron BA.2 variants. Our initial Alpha, Beta, and Gamma viral stocks contained ~50% of the nsp6ΔSGF variant, which increased in proportion over time when grown in human airway cells, paralleling the real-world data. nsp6ΔSGF has been reported to enhance ER zippering and double membrane vesicle clustering,63 which, along with multiple independent selections, suggest a fitness advantage. In a mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection, a similar mutation (nsp6ΔLSG) was associated with viral attenuation in combination with a nsp6 I189V mutation, possibly indicating a species dependent effect.64 Our competition experiments revealed apparent recombination events favoring mutations in the 3’ end of viruses from the B.1.617.1 lineage (Kappa). In particular, the N R203M mutation was favored, with a concomitant disfavoring of the N R203K/G204R mutation. The KR mutation, found in Alpha and Gamma variants, has been described to increase replication and fitness of SARS-CoV-2.65,66 N R203K has also been linked to effects on viral assembly and packaging in viral-like particles.67 However, our data suggests that N R203M may be favored in primary human airway epithelia.

As fitness is a complex trait composed of many different elements, it can be difficult to assess the causes of increased fitness in human populations. The increased fitness of SARS-CoV-2 variants in the human population, especially Alpha, Delta, and Omicron, was obvious as each displaced preexisting strains. However, it is difficult to know from case data why these variants in particular were globally successful and not others. Three of the major components of fitness are replicative fitness (viral growth), transmission, and antigenic fitness. Each trait is dependent upon virus-host selection pressures across populations. To assess replicative fitness directly through a controlled experiment, we performed head-to-head competitions of SARS-CoV-2 variants in primary cells. By this assay, we determined that Gamma and Delta were able to outcompete the other variants, consistent with greater replicative fitness.68 We performed additional competitions with Spike-exchanged chimeric viruses, and observed different results for Beta, Gamma, and Delta, indicating that mutations outside of Spike are also important for viral growth and adaptation. Several non-structural mutations which arose in SARS-CoV-2 variants are detailed above; additionally, mutations can be designed which have much greater effects in primary culture and animal models compared to immortalized cell culture models.69

The high replicative fitness of Delta is concordant with real-world data; however, the high replicative fitness observed for Gamma was surprising. Originally arising in Brazil, Gamma did not spread greatly outside of South America, and was later replaced by Delta.70 This observation suggests that other forms of fitness overshadowed the replicative fitness of Gamma, including a reported greater transmissibility of Delta.71 There is also a possibility that host genetics could partially explain the relative geographical restriction of Gamma, as we observed variant-specific differences in the ability to infect cells from different patient donors.72–74 The widespread success of the Delta variant likely reflects high fitness of multiple types - replicative, transmissive, and antigenic. Our study has demonstrated high replicative fitness for Delta with low variance on different genetic backgrounds, and there is evidence to suggest greater transmission.75 Additionally, Delta displays reduced neutralization compared to D614G in human pre-immune sera (Supplemental Figure 5B), and higher frequencies of breakthrough infections have been observed.76,77

In contrast, Omicron (BA.1) displayed reduced replicative fitness in primary human cells compared to the other variants, suggesting that the global spread of Omicron was due to enhanced transmissibility and altered antigenicity, not replication. Interestingly, although experiments in animal models have indicated reduced transmissibility with Omicron,78 the effective reproductive number of Omicron in the human population is higher than Delta.79 Although it is indirect evidence, initial rapid acceleration of viral growth observed in Omicron infected HNE cells in this study and others80 may position this strain for increased transmissibility, while the reduced growth phenotypes in SAE and alveolarspheres may attenuate its pathogenic potential compared to earlier variants. The antigenic differences observed in Omicron strains have been well-studied, and vaccine protection against Omicron was significantly reduced compared to other variants.36,77,81 Overall, these data lead to a model wherein the first Omicron sublineage to emerge, BA.1 (used in this study), evolved a novel antigenic base, which was probably the major initial contributor to its success in human populations. This model is supported by evidence from epidemiological studies, and the finding that vaccinated individuals/animals transmit Omicron more effectively than unvaccinated.82,83 As we have now seen, successive sublineages quickly replaced BA.1, most likely due to rounds of adaptation and increased replicative fitness on this base. In fact, the later Omicron sublineage BA.5 has been reported to have increased fitness and reduced innate immune induction relative to BA.1, supporting this hypothesis.84,85

sec.title: LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY
sec.p: Sample sizes of the primary human airway cultures used in this study are limited (n=3–4) due to tissue availability, and, as such, are not representative of the entire human population. Matched patient codes were used whenever possible. This model cannot recapitulate organismal level disease progression or transmission and does not incorporate adaptive immune responses. As no SARS-CoV-2 variant is defined by a single sequence, the patient isolate strains used in this study are not necessarily representative of every viral strain of that variant, and strain differences complicate comparison with other reported results. In the scope of this work we were not able to determine which individual mutations were responsible for the observed replication and fitness phenotypes. Further work will be needed to elucidate mechanisms of viral fitness.

sec.title: BIOSAFETY STATEMENT
sec.p: All work with SARS-CoV-2 was performed in an accredited BSL3 laboratory at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and experiments were approved by the UNC Institutional Biosafety Committee. All personnel wear Tyvek suits, aprons, booties, double gloves, hoods and HEPA filtered Powered Air Purifying Respirators in BSL3 conditions. Samples resulting from the competition studies were immediately inactivated using approved methods or destroyed. Spike replacements were generated on a virus backbone where ORF7a was removed and replaced with nanoLuciferase as an additional precaution. Creation and use of these viruses was approved by the UNC Institutional Biosafety Committee and the National Institutes of Health.

sec.title: Large airway epithelial (LAE) cells:
sec.p: Human bronchial epithelial (LAE) cells were isolated from freshly excised normal human lungs obtained from transplant donors with lungs unsuitable for transplant under IRB-approved protocol (#03–1396), as previously described.86,87 LAE cells were expanded using the conditionally reprogrammed cell (CRC) method88 and then cultured on porous Transwell (Corning) supports in ALI media (50:50 LHC:DMEM-H supplemented with 0.5 ng/mL EGF and 1 mM CaCl2). Upon confluence, cells were maintained at an ALI by removing apical media and providing ALI media to the basal compartment only. Cells were grown at 37°C in a humidified environment with 5% CO2. Cultures used for electron microscopy were maintained in PneumaCult ALI media. After 28 days, LAE cells were used for infections.

sec.title: Viral growth curves
sec.p: Primary LAE, SAE, and HNE cultures were infected on the apical side with MOI=0.1 in 200 uL total inoculum (1X PBS) for 1.5 hours, followed by removal of the inoculum and 3× 500 uL 1X PBS washes. The last wash was collected for the 0hr timepoint. Apical washes were performed every 24 hours for 96 hours, by adding 200 uL of 1X PBS to the apical side and incubating for 10 minutes. Media was replaced in the basal compartment at the halfway point of the experiment. Apical washes were titered by plaque assay

Organoid cultures were infected with 200 uL of equal viral load for 1.5 hours, followed by removal of the inoculum and 3× 1X PBS washes, then replacement with culture media. 200 uL of supernatant was collected every 24 hours for 96 hours, and titered by plaque assay.

sec.title: Whole-mount immunostaining and imaging
sec.p: SARS-CoV-2 infected ALI cultures were fixed twice for 20 minutes in 4% formaldehyde in PBS and stored in PBS. Cultures were stained for the SARS-CoV N protein (0.5 ug/mL), a-tubulin (3ug/mL) and CCSP (1:3000) using species-specific secondary antibodies.91 Nuclei were visualized with Hoechst 33342 staining. A Stellaris 5 (Leica) confocal microscope was used to acquire 5-channel Z stacks. Representative stacks are shown as XZ cross sections to distinguish individual cell features and to characterize the infected cell types. ImageJ was used to measure the relative apical culture surface covered by SARS-CoV-2 N, a-tubulin, or CCSP signal.

sec.title: RNAScope
sec.p: Primary LAE and SAE cultures from the terminal timepoint of viral growth curves were washed twice with PBS, then dissociated with Accutase for 30 minutes at 37C. Dissociated cells were recovered, spun at 300xg to pellet, and resuspended in DMEM with 10% FBS. Resuspended cells were filtered for single cells in a 40 μm strainer, spun at 300xg to pellet, and resuspended in 4% formaldehyde. After fixation, dissociated cells were washed with PBS 3x and cytocentrifuged on slide glasses (55 g, 4 min, StatSpin CytoFuge2, Beckman Coulter). The cytocentrifuged cells on the slide glasses were dehydrated with graded ethanol (50% 1 min, 70% 1 min, 100% 1 min). The slides were stored in 100% ethanol at −20°C until future use for RNA-ISH. RNA-ISH was performed on cytocentrifuged single cells using the RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent Assay v2, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cytospin slides were rehydrated with graded ethanol (100% 1 min, 70% 1 min, 50% 1 min), permeabilized with PBS + 0.1% Tween 20 (PBST) at RT for 10 min, incubated with hydrogen peroxide at RT for 10 min, followed by incubation with 1:15 diluted protease III at RT for 10 min. Slides were hybridized with custom probes at 40°C for 2 hours, and signals were amplified according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The stained slides were scanned and digitized using an Olympus VS200 fluorescent microscope. RNA-ISH was performed on cytocentrifuged single cells using RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent Assay v2, as described above, to assess colocalization of SARS-CoV-2 Spike transcript and ciliated (FOXJ1) or secretory (SCGB1A1) cell marker transcripts. Using Fiji software,92 quantification for colocalization was performed in the scanned images by an investigator blinded to slide identification. For quantitative co-localization analysis of SARS-CoV-2 Spike transcript with airway epithelial markers, 200 cells expressing SARS-CoV-2 Spike transcript were examined for co-expression of FOXJ1 and SCGB1A1. Proportions of airway epithelial cell marker-positive cells among SARS-CoV-2 transcript-positive cells were shown.

sec.title: Scanning Electron Microscopy
sec.p: As previously published,93,94 cultures were gently submerged in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1M sodium cacodylate buffer overnight at 4°C and rinsed twice with 4% PFA. Samples were rinsed with 0.1M sodium cacodylate buffer to remove any fixative before osmication and dehydration. For osmium tetroxide fixation (OTO), samples were gently submerged in a solution of 1% OsO4 in deionized water for 1h. Samples were washed 5X for 5 min with deionized water to remove the osmium solution before submerging in filtered 1% tannic acid in deionized water for 30 min. Samples were washed again with deionized water to remove the tannic acid solution and then submerged in 1% OsO4 for 15 min. Fixed cultures were then rinsed 3X for 5 min with diH2O. Subsequently, samples were dehydrated in 6X 10 min baths of increasing concentrations of ethanol (30%, 50%, 75%, 95%, 100%, 100%) and dried using a Samdri-795 liquid CO2 critical point drier (Tousimis Research Corp). Following drying, samples were mounted on aluminum planchets with carbon adhesive tabs (cell inserts) and coated with 5 nm gold palladium alloy (60Au:40Pd) using a Ted Pella 208HR sputter coater (Ted Pella Inc). Samples were imaged using a Supra 25 field emission scanning electron microscope operating at 5kV with a working distance of 5 mm and 30 μm aperture (Carl Zeiss Microscopy).

sec.title: Transmission Electron Microscopy
sec.p: Cultures were gently submerged in 4% paraformaldehyde and 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate as previously described.6,93 Samples were rinsed with sodium cacodylate buffer and were post-fixed for 1h in potassium-ferrocyanide reduced osmium (1% osmium tetroxide/1.25% potassium ferrocyanide/0.1 sodium cacodylate buffer). After rinsing in deionized water, the cells were dehydrated using increasing concentrations of ethanol (30%, 50%, 75%, 90%, 100%, 100%, 10 minutes each) followed by infiltration and embedment in Polybed 812 epoxy resin. The cells/transwell inserts were sectioned perpendicular to the substrate at 70nm using a diamond knife and Leica UCT ultramicrotome. Ultrathin sections were collected on 200 mesh copper grids and stained with 4% aqueous uranyl acetate for 15 minutes, followed by Reynolds’ lead citrate for 7 minutes. Samples were observed using a FEI Tecnai 12 transmission electron microscope operating at 120kV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and images were taken using a Gatan Orius SC1000 CCD camera with Gatan Microscopy Suite 3.0 software).

sec.title: Cytotoxicity assay
sec.p: Apical washes from viral growth curves were analyzed for LDH release using the LDH-Glo Cytotoxicity Assay following the manufacturer’s instructions. Percent cytotoxicity was calculated relative to a maximum LDH release control, consisting of the apical wash from a Triton X-100 treated HAE culture as described in the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: scRNA-seq
sec.p: Primary LAE and SAE cultures from the terminal timepoint of viral growth curves were washed twice with PBS, then dissociated with Accutase for 30 minutes at 37C. Dissociated cells were recovered, spun at 300xg to pellet, and resuspended in DMEM with 10% FBS. Resuspended cells were filtered for single cells in a 40 μm strainer, spun at 300xg to pellet, and resuspended in Bambanker freezing media. Resuspended cells were slowly frozen to −80C. On the day of single-cell sequencing preparation, cells were thawed, spun at 300xg to pellet, and resuspended in 1xPBS at a target concentration of 1e6 cells/mL, and used for GEM generation on the 10X Genomics platform using the Chromium Next GEM single Cell 3’ Reagent Kit v3.1. Prepared libraries were validated on a BioAnalyzer (Agilent), and libraries were sequenced by the UNC High Throughput Sequencing Core.

Raw data in FASTQ formats were pre-processed using cellranger v6.1.2 standard count pipeline per sample against custom reference human genome plus SARS-CoV-2 genome (NC_045512), with Gencode human gene annotation release v37, and ENSEMBL SARS-CoV-2 gene annotations v101. Positive strand viral open reading frames (ORF) were used as gene boundaries; therefore, ORF1ab represents the canonical genomic RNA, and the last known expressed 3’-canonical sub-genomic, N for nucleocapsid protein, represent the total viral RNA. Gene count matrices from cellranger pipeline outputs were loaded into RStudio environment with Seurat v495 using recommended quality control parameters after ambient RNA decontamination with the R package SoupX96, and doublet removal using the Bioconductor R package scDblFinder.97 The data were stored as Seurat objects and combined through the data integration routine and saved as R data set (.rds) for subsequent analysis. Cell type clusters, marker gene differential expression analysis, and various plots commonly used for single cell data presentation were generated based on recommended protocols from Seurat. Differential gene expression analysis among different experimental conditions were performed using the R package MAST.98 MAST performs Hurdle tests that combine logistic regression for discrete expression yes/no per gene, and mean expression differences among positive cells. Functional gene set enrichment or over-representation analysis were performed using the Bioconductor R package fgsea,99 against gene sets or pathways constructed from Gene Ontology (Biological Processes), or Reactome. Various plots were generated with the help with Bioconductor R package ComplexHeatmap, ggplot2, and plotly.100–102

sec.title: RNA sequencing
sec.p: Viral genomes were extracted from apical washes were extracted using TRIzol LS, following the manufacturer’s protocol. 100ng of total RNA was used as input for the Illumina Stranded Total RNA Prep with Ribo-Zero Plus protocol. Libraries were prepared for sequencing on a MiSeq instrument following the manufacturer’s protocol and sequenced on a 150v3 chip with at least 500,000 reads per sample. Reads were aligned to the SARS-CoV-2 WA1 genome using STAR with the parameters --peOverlapNbasesMin 30 --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate. BAM files were imported into Geneious Prime and variants with >100 read coverage and >2% frequency were called. Data from replicates were averaged and graphed using R. To determine the relative mutation load (RML) metric, the frequencies of all identified mutations were summed (∑i=1i=nfi).

sec.title: Competition assays
sec.p: A 1:1 MOI mixture of the indicated viruses (total MOI=0.01) was used to infect primary LAE and SAE cultures as described above. Viral stocks used were matched for cell type used for production. Apical washes at the terminal timepoint of each experiment were used to perform plaque assays to titer viral growth. Viral gRNA was extracted from the inoculum, and from apical washes performed at the indicated timepoints using TRIzol LS following the manufacturer’s protocol. DdPCR was used to quantify the relative quantities of each variant in the population using the Bio-Rad One-Step RT-ddPCR Advanced Kit for Probes and QX200 AutoDG Droplet Digital PCR System. Instructions from the Bio-Rad SARS-CoV-2 ddPCR Kit were used to set up reactions with the following probe sets: B.1.1.7 (HV 69–70 deletion), B.1.35.1 (D80A or K417N), P.1 (K417T), B.1.617 (L452R), B.1.1.529 (N856K), and N501Y.

sec.title: Neutralization assay
sec.p: Neutralization assays were conducted full-length live reporter virus with the nano-luciferase (nLuc) reporter gene replacing ORF7a as previously reported.26,103,104 Heat-inactivated serum samples were initially diluted 1:20 then serially diluted 5-fold down a 96 well plate in virus growth medium (1X MEM, 5% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin before transfer to the BSL3 laboratory. In the BSL3 laboratory, nLuc viruses were diluted in virus growth medium, added in equal volume to serum dilution plates, and incubated for 1hr at 37°C, 5% CO2. The virus and serum dilutions were then added to duplicate columns of a 96 well black plate seeded one day prior to use with 2×104 Vero E6 cells per well, for a final virus dilution of 800 Plaque Forming Units (PFU) per well, and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. After 24hrs, virus was quantified with the Promega Nano-Glo Luciferase Assay system with a Promega GloMax Explorer. Inhibitory Dose 50 (ID50) titer was defined as the serum dilution at which the observed Relative Light Units (RLU) were reduced by 50%, when compared to Virus+Cell and Virus only control wells, as determined by an Excel macro and analyzed using GraphPad Prism.

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was carried out using Graphpad Prism version 9.1 using Student’s t-test or 1-way ANOVA. Significance symbols are defined as follow: * p<0.05, ** p< 0.01, *** p<0.001, **** p<0.0001. Data are graphed as mean +/− standard deviation. Information about n number and statistical tests can be found in the figure legends.

caption.p: Growth kinetics and morphology of SARS-CoV-2 variants in primary airway cultures. A) Growth curve of the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants on primary human nasal epithelia (HNE) cells (MOI=0.1; n=3 patient codes). Data are plotted as mean +/− SEM. B) Growth curve of the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants on primary human large airway epithelia (LAE) cells (MOI=0.1; n=3–4 patient codes). Data are plotted as mean +/− SEM. C) Growth curve of the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants on primary human small airway epithelia (SAE) cells (MOI=0.01; n=3–4 patient codes). Data are plotted as mean +/− SEM. A 2-way ANOVA with repeated measures and multiple comparisons, in comparison to D614G, was used for statistical analysis. * = p <0.05. D) Growth curve of the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants on primary human AT2 alveolosphere organoids (n=2 patient codes). Data are plotted as mean +/− SEM. A 2-way ANOVA with repeated measures and multiple comparisons, in comparison to D614G, was used for statistical analysis. * = p <0.05. E) Growth curve of the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants on A549-hACE2 cells (n=3). Data are plotted as mean +/− SEM. A 2-way ANOVA with repeated measures and multiple comparisons, in comparison to D614G, was used for statistical analysis. * = p <0.05. F) RNAScope was performed on LAE/SAE cultures harvested at 96 hpi after the above-described growth curves (n=3–4 patient codes) with the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants. FOXJ1 is a marker of ciliated cells, and SCGB1A1 is a marker of secretory cells. G) Whole mount cultures at 96 hpi after the above described growth curves (n=3–4 patient codes) were stained for viral antigen. The percent area with viral staining, quantified by whole membrane scan, is shown for LAE (left) and SAE (right) cells. Individual data points are shown, with each color representing a different donor code. Data are plotted as mean +/− SD. Student’s t-test was used for statistical analysis, in comparison to D614G. * = p <0.05. H) Whole mount cultures at 96 hpi were stained for viral antigen (green), α-tubulin (white), CCSP (red), and nuclei (blue). α-tubulin is a marker of ciliated cells, and CCSP is a marker of secretory cells. Arrow: α-tubulin+ ciliated cells; *: α -tubulin+/CCSP+ cells; #: CCSP+ squamous cells; ^: α -tubulin−/CCSP− cells. Scale bar = 25μm. I) Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, left) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, right) of LAE cells at 72 hpi with the indicated SARS-CoV-2 variants.
